actions.justification: Mandatory first step: assess current vital signs to establish baseline and guide resuscitation in this patient presenting with hematemesis and melena (HR 105, BP 120/80).
Mandatory: evaluate hemodynamic stability including orthostatic changes, perfusion, and signs of shock in the setting of acute upper GI bleed.
Mandatory: large-bore IV access is essential for fluid resuscitation and potential blood product transfusion in acute GI bleeding.
Mandatory lab to assess hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelet count in a patient with active GI bleeding (hematemesis and melena). Critical for determining transfusion need and severity of blood loss.
Mandatory coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) to assess bleeding risk and guide management of hematemesis/melena. Required before procedural interventions.
Mandatory type and crossmatch in anticipation of possible packed RBC transfusion given active upper GI bleeding with tachycardia (HR 105).
BMP needed to assess electrolytes, BUN/creatinine (BUN:creatinine ratio helps confirm GI bleeding source), and renal function in this patient with hematemesis and melena.
Repeat CBC to trend hemoglobin given active GI bleeding; initial CBC may not reflect true blood loss in acute hemorrhage.
GI consultation is essential for urgent upper endoscopy (EGD) evaluation and management of suspected upper GI bleed (hematemesis + melena).
Patient is tachycardic (HR 105) with active GI bleeding; IV crystalloid bolus is indicated for hemodynamic resuscitation to maintain perfusion while awaiting blood products and endoscopy.
IV proton pump inhibitor (e.g., pantoprazole infusion) is standard of care for upper GI bleeding to stabilize clot formation and reduce rebleeding risk prior to endoscopy.
Prokinetic agent (e.g., IV erythromycin or metoclopramide) administered pre-endoscopy promotes gastric emptying and clears blood from the stomach, improving visualization during endoscopy.
Patient with hematemesis and melena, HR 105 suggesting possible hemodynamic compromise. Lactate will help assess tissue perfusion and severity of bleeding, guiding resuscitation decisions.
Patient has active GI bleeding with hematemesis and melena. Type and crossmatch is essential to prepare packed RBCs for potential transfusion if hemoglobin returns below 7 g/dL.
In upper GI bleeding with suspected variceal or peptic source, octreotide reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure, decreasing bleeding risk. Appropriate adjunct while awaiting endoscopy.

Patient has hematemesis and melena with tachycardia (HR 105). CBC is pending but a repeat CBC is needed to trend hemoglobin and guide transfusion decisions (transfuse if Hgb <7). This is distinct from the already-completed order_lab_cbc_repeat and will help assess ongoing bleeding.

Repeat lactate to assess tissue perfusion and severity of bleeding. Tachycardia with GI bleed raises concern for occult hemodynamic compromise despite relatively preserved BP (MAP 73). Trending lactate guides resuscitation adequacy.

Patient with upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) and tachycardia warrants early surgical consultation in case endoscopic management fails or if bleeding source requires surgical intervention. Early involvement improves readiness for escalation.

Patient with hematemesis and melena, HR 105 suggesting ongoing blood loss. Transfusion threshold of Hgb <7 is standard of care for upper GI bleeding per guidelines. CBC is pending but clinical picture warrants preparation for transfusion.
CT abdomen can help identify the source of GI bleeding (e.g., varices, ulcer, vascular malformation) and guide further management including potential angiography or surgical intervention.

Patient with hematemesis and melena who has had initial resuscitation, labs ordered, and GI/surgery consulted. Angiography can help localize the source of GI bleeding and may serve as both diagnostic and therapeutic (embolization) if endoscopy is delayed or if the bleeding source is unclear. Given the tachycardia (HR 105) suggesting ongoing or recent significant hemorrhage, angiography is clinically appropriate at this stage.
